name: Chuka
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: Only dialect-comparison paper (Erastus 2011, NJAS) surfaced; no stress statement reachable

sources.citation: Ford, K. C. 1976. Tone in Kikamba and the Central Kenya Bantu languages. Studies in African Linguistics 7(3): 261-293.
sources.note: First-hand tone data for Cuka (informant Mutegi Mbungu, p. 261 fn. 1): two tone levels expandable to four (extra-high/extra-low), Cuka tone-form classes (12) p. 268, sentence tones p. 270, 'Only one other dialect, Cuka, has a comparable process [to Kikuyu high-tone spreading]' p. 270, comparative verb tones pp. 278ff. The words stress/accent never occur.

sources.citation: Mbaka, Nancy W. 2016. Vowel epenthesis as a parameter setting strategy in Gichuka loanwords. In Isutsa & Githae (eds.), Proceedings of the Second Chuka University International Research Conference, 431-441. Chuka University.
sources.note: Government Phonology analysis of English loanword epenthesis; nothing on stress or tone.

sources.citation: Starzmann, Paul M. 2016. Inheritance and contact in Central Kenya Bantu: A dialectological approach. PhD dissertation, Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin. 609 pp. (Glottolog ref 667965; Chuka one of 18 sampled varieties)
sources.note: Segmental and lexical dialectology (530 mentions of Chuka); 'tone/tonal' occurs only in a bibliography entry and 'stress' only in non-Bantu contexts (English flapping rule, 'accent-free' contact). Silent on Chuka prosody.

sources.citation: Muriungi, Peter Kinyua, Miriam Kathomi Mutegi & Mary Karuri. 2014. The syntax of wh-questions in Gichuka. Open Journal of Modern Linguistics 4(1): 182-204. doi:10.4236/ojml.2014.41015 (CC BY). (Glottolog ref 573308)
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Syntax only; no phonology, tone or stress statement (Clements & Ford 1979 on Kikuyu tone appears only in the bibliography).

sources.citation: Ndwiga, Silvano Murithi. 2014. The syntax and pragmatics of the Gichuka sentence: A challenge to the minimalist program analysis. PhD thesis, University of Nairobi. 309 pp. (Glottolog ref 471693)
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Syntax/pragmatics; §1.1 'Background to the language' (pp. 1-2) is sociolinguistic only; the word 'tone' never occurs; 'stress' appears only as a syntactic feature [+stress]. Silent.

sources.citation: Kanana, Fridah E. 2011. Dialect convergence and divergence: A case of Chuka and Imenti. In Bokamba, Shosted & Ayalew (eds.), Selected Proceedings of the 40th Annual Conference on African Linguistics, 190-205. Somerville, MA: Cascadilla. (Glottolog ref 94773, listed by Glottolog as a comparative study;phonology)
sources.note: Segmental comparison only (vowels, consonants, Dahl's law, /ɣ/-/β/-/r/ retention, noun-class morphophonemics); no tone description. The only prosodic remark is fn. 10, p. 200: 'Sometimes the speakers stress the final vowels to produce a very long vowel' — emphatic vowel lengthening, not a word-stress rule.
sources.venue: Selected Proceedings of the 40th Annual Conference on African Linguistics
